role: Low-level, hardware-agnostic Rust interface over NVIDIA, AMD, Apple, Qualcomm, Intel, Google, and AWS accelerators plus Vulkan/D3D12/OpenGL/WebGPU. Agent-first: predictable shapes, terse APIs, errors that name the failing operation. Includes a faster drop-in replacement for cudarc.

capabilities.name: allocation.as_ptr
capabilities.description:
Raw device pointer. Backends that virtualise pointers return a \
 handle cast to a raw pointer, so it is not always dereferenceable \
 on the host. Declares: unchecked.

note: requires_grant and budgeted are now DERIVED from the effects the crate declares per operation. An earlier version of this file said both were judgement, which was true before the ontology module existed. The effect set is deliberately not a read_only boolean. On a device the authority to use it and the cost of using it are the same resource, so the operations that allocate, execute, compile or transfer are both granted and budgeted together -- an alignment that would look like a mistake elsewhere in this stack and is correct here. compute.pipeline is granted for a distinct reason and declares `compiles` rather than `executes`: it turns caller-supplied bytes into device instructions without running them. A caller gating only on execution would let arbitrary program text reach the device unexamined, and a test pins the two apart. allocation.as_ptr is the one operation granted without consuming anything. It hands out a raw pointer -- which backends that virtualise pointers return as a handle, not a dereferenceable host address -- and it is the only member of the `unchecked` set. A test asserts that set stays exactly one entry, because this crate trades guard-rails for throughput by design and each further trade should be reviewed as one. Unlike the CLI tools in this stack, this ontology is hand-maintained: Rust offers no reflection over trait methods, so no drift test can walk the real surface the way clap allows. Adding a trait method without declaring it here will not fail a build. The module says so in its own preamble rather than implying a guarantee it cannot make.`unmapped` was added 2026-09-15: this file had been silent about what it leaves out, which NS-ONTO-001 2.5 requires and `ironstack verify` had reported on every run. The first entry is the one a reader most needs -- this crate states in its own module documentation that it prioritises throughput over guard-rails and exposes `_unchecked` fast paths, and a published surface that did not repeat that would be advertising 27 capabilities on terms the manifest never mentioned.

unmapped.area: memory safety on the fast path
unmapped.why: This crate prioritises throughput over guard-rails, deliberately and in its own words. Where a safe wrapper would add bounds checks, allocation tracking or synchronous teardown, the `_unchecked` variants do not, and the caller opts back into safety rather than out of it. An out-of-bounds launch geometry or a pointer outliving its allocation is undefined behaviour on a device, and nothing here will report it -- which is the trade a driver substrate makes and is worth saying rather than discovering.

Workload descriptors, execution-strategy selection, tensor descriptors, quantization schemes and CPU reference kernels are IronWorks'. This defines the trait surface every backend implements and the vendor-neutral description of what a driver owns -- devices, capability bits, memory, streams, events, launch geometry -- and nothing that decides what to run.

unmapped.area: what a backend actually does with a call
unmapped.why: There are no backend bindings in this crate at all. It is the surface; CUDA, ROCm, Metal and the NPU backends implement it elsewhere, and whether one honours the contract is established by that backend's own tests rather than here. A capability bit says what a device claims, not what it delivers.

Descriptions are vendor-neutral and compiled without a driver on the machine. A capability described here may be unavailable, absent or belong to hardware nobody has plugged in, and the difference between `this substrate can express it` and `this machine can do it` is a question for a running backend.
